chunks.section: Same Function, Different Gradients: Evaluating Gradient Reliability under Reparameterization
chunks.text: Bum Jun Kim † † thanks: Corresponding author Affiliation: The University of Tokyo Email: bumjun.kim@weblab.t.u-tokyo.ac.jp

Gradients are no longer used only to train models: Gradient magnitudes are now measurement instruments, used to rank attention heads for pruning, to decide per-example clipping in private training, to allocate adapter rank budgets, and to debug models. Across these workflows, larger gradient magnitudes are taken to mean greater importance. Even for a fixed input–output function, these gradients are computed in one of many possible parameter coordinate systems. For example, attention scores depend on the query and key projections only through the paired product W Q ​ W K ⊤ W_{Q}W_{K}^{\top} . Scaling a head’s query projection by c c and the corresponding key projection by 1 / c 1/c therefore leaves every output logit unchanged. This change in parameter coordinates rescales the corresponding query and key gradient norms by 1 / c 1/c and c c , respectively. To test whether gradient-based decisions remain unchanged under these coordinate changes, we introduce Gradient Reliability under Reparameterization (GRR). GRR rewrites a trained model in new parameter coordinates that compute exactly the same function, verifies that predictions are unchanged, and then tests whether the decisions derived from the gradients are unchanged too. Our audits span GLUE classifiers, a ViT on CIFAR-10, GPT-2-medium and GPT-2-large, a 1.1B-parameter Llama-style model on WikiText-2, and six trained LoRA adapters. Empirically, predictions are preserved throughout, but both the gradients and the gradient-based decisions change. Across 66 GLUE attention audits, the median top-3 overlap of raw head-gradient rankings is only 1 / 3 1/3 , and rankings and pruning masks change even under the mildest rescalings we test. In the largest of 14 global-pruning audits, the shifted ranking selects head masks that differ in four of 22 pruned heads and reach 50.92 % 50.92\% and 94.84 % 94.84\% validation accuracy on one ELECTRA SST-2 model. We prove that same-function reparameterizations can realize any component ranking and make gradient scores arbitrarily large, so these gradient-based measurements are not properties of the learned function at all. Beyond diagnosis, we propose symmetry-aware remedies: Function-space controls and canonical balancing restore identical decisions in every audit we run, and a quotient-space score is provably invariant under any invertible change of basis in the low-rank factors. Gradient-based evidence must therefore be verified to remain unchanged under same-function reparameterization, or be independent of coordinate choice by definition; otherwise, the evidence cannot be trusted.

Gradients are used for more than model training. Quantities derived from gradients have become general-purpose measurement tools, used for structured pruning ( Michel et al., 2019 ; Molchanov et al., 2017 ) , compression of large language models ( Ma et al., 2023 ) , differential privacy clipping ( Abadi et al., 2016 ) , low-rank adaptation (LoRA) rank allocation ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) , and model debugging through training-example influence ( Koh and Liang, 2017 ; Grosse et al., 2023 ) . These workflows convert parameter, activation, or mask derivatives into scalar scores—often norms or Taylor sensitivities—that decide which components are pruned, which examples are clipped or flagged, and how rank budgets are allocated. These scores are treated as evidence of what matters to the represented input–output function. Figure 1: Overview of the GRR audit. Scaling a head’s query projection by c c and the corresponding key projection by 1 / c 1/c preserves the model’s function and predictions. This coordinate change rescales the query and key gradients by 1 / c 1/c and c c , respectively. Applying different scales across heads changes the raw-gradient head ranking. Gradient-guided pruning therefore keeps different heads, and the two pruned ELECTRA models differ substantially in SST-2 validation accuracy, as detailed in Sec. 4.3 .

Yet each such score is computed in a particular coordinate system on the network’s parameters. The choice matters because parameter gradients depend on the coordinates even when the input–output function is fixed. Raw gradient scores therefore reflect the coordinate choice as well as the represented function. Neural-network parameter spaces classically admit transformations that leave the input–output map unchanged ( Hecht-Nielsen, 1990 ) . If a differentiable, locally invertible transformation T : Θ → Θ T:\Theta\to\Theta of the parameter space Θ \Theta satisfies f T ⁡ ( θ ) ​ ( x ) = f θ ​ ( x ) f_{T(\theta)}(x)=f_{\theta}(x) for every input x ∈ 𝒳 x\in\mathcal{X} , then T T is a function-preserving reparameterization, and the differential of the loss is transported by the chain rule, ∇ θ ′ ℒ = ( D ​ T − 1 ​ ( θ ′ ) ) ⊤ ​ ∇ θ ℒ , θ ′ ≔ T ⁡ ( θ ) . \nabla_{\theta^{\prime}}\mathcal{L}=(DT^{-1}(\theta^{\prime}))^{\top}\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L},\qquad\theta^{\prime}\coloneqq T(\theta). (1) Common gradient-based measurements are computed in a chosen Euclidean coordinate system. The resulting quantities and decisions, including gradient norms, coordinate-wise Taylor scores, diagonal Fisher estimates, clipping decisions, and top- k k rankings, can change with the coordinates. The function is unchanged by T T , but the coordinate representation of the parameter gradient can change, as can scores computed from that representation. An orbit is the set of parameter vectors reachable from one model through the chosen function-preserving transformations. These vectors represent the same input–output function in different parameter coordinates.

For example, Transformer attention admits such a function-preserving reparameterization. Attention scores depend on the query and key projections only through the paired product W Q ​ W K ⊤ W_{Q}W_{K}^{\top} , so replacing ( W Q , h , W K , h ) (W_{Q,h},W_{K,h}) by ( c h ​ W Q , h , c h − 1 ​ W K , h ) (c_{h}W_{Q,h},c_{h}^{-1}W_{K,h}) leaves every output logit unchanged while scaling the two head-gradient norms by c h − 1 c_{h}^{-1} and c h c_{h} . The head still attends to the same tokens and contributes the same output. Only the units used to measure the head have changed, but this coordinate change rescales the head’s parameter gradients. By choosing c h c_{h} , we can make the same head report an arbitrarily large gradient score without changing any prediction. The represented function therefore does not uniquely determine this raw gradient score—a failure of identifiability, not of measurement precision. We must therefore reassess the reliability of gradient-based evidence: Gradient norms, head rankings, clipping decisions, and rank budgets must be audited under coordinate changes that preserve the function. Input-side attributions are unaffected, since these attributions are determined by the function alone ( Sundararajan et al., 2017 ) .

chunks.section: Same-function coordinate changes occur in practice.
chunks.text: Data-free quantization equalizes weight ranges across adjacent layers, post-training quantization migrates activation scale into the paired weight matrix, and structured slicing rotates the internal representation before deleting rows and columns ( Nagel et al., 2019 ; Xiao et al., 2023 ; Ashkboos et al., 2024 ) . Each of these steps preserves the represented function and changes only how that function is written down. Compression pipelines routinely chain such a step with a gradient-based pruning or rank-allocation step, so the gradient evidence consumed downstream is read in a coordinate that an earlier and purely functional optimization happened to choose. No deliberate transformation is even required to produce scale imbalance. The eight public checkpoints we audit already have unequal paired projection norms: Balancing the paired projections within each checkpoint’s orbit requires scales in [ 0.837 , 1.077 ] [0.837,1.077] . The coordinate choice underlying gradient evidence is therefore already arbitrary.

chunks.section: Same-function coordinate changes occur in practice.
chunks.text: To test whether gradient-based decisions remain unchanged under such coordinate changes, we introduce Gradient Reliability under Reparameterization (GRR): The audit holds the represented input–output function fixed, changes only the parameter coordinates, and tests whether the measurements read from the gradients—and the decisions those measurements drive—remain unchanged. We instantiate this invariance check with exact Transformer symmetries and verify forward preservation by checking that the two coordinates produce numerically identical outputs. We then examine gradient evidence and compare downstream decisions such as pruning masks, clipping labels, LoRA rank choices, and paired-product optimizer diagnostics. In the largest of our global GLUE pruning audits, two same-function coordinates of one ELECTRA SST-2 model make identical predictions, yet the pruning decisions differ sharply: The raw gradient ranking selects head masks that differ in four of the 22 pruned heads, and the two pruned models reach 50.92 % 50.92\% and 94.84 % 94.84\% validation accuracy. Figure 1 illustrates this audit. GRR holds the represented function fixed and tests whether an existing diagnostic and the corresponding downstream decision are well defined along exact symmetry orbits. We also propose symmetry-aware remedies. Function-space ablation, a path-normalized score, and canonical balancing make the two coordinates select identical decisions in every audit we run. A quotient-space score remains unchanged under any invertible change of basis in the low-rank factors. These remedies provide a drop-in replacement for a diagnostic that fails the audit.

That Euclidean gradients depend on coordinates is classical ( Amari, 1998 ; Martens, 2020 ) , and prior work has used the freedom to change parameter coordinates in three ways: to question generalization claims such as flatness ( Dinh et al., 2017 ) , to design scores that are invariant by construction ( Neyshabur et al., 2015 ; Tanaka et al., 2020 ) , and to exploit motion along symmetry orbits as an optimization resource ( Kunin et al., 2021 ; Zhao et al., 2022 ) . Reliability tests for explanations are closest in spirit, but existing tests perturb the model ( Adebayo et al., 2018 ) or the input ( Kindermans et al., 2019 ) and test whether the explanation notices. GRR applies a complementary test: The audit leaves the model’s behavior exactly intact, verified numerically before any gradient is computed, and tests whether a diagnostic that a pipeline already executes still returns the same decision. Correspondingly, every strict ordering of raw component scores is attainable on a single same-function orbit, and the attainable score ranges have no finite upper bound. To the best of our knowledge, the effects of these coordinate changes on downstream gradient evidence and decisions have not been systematically audited. Exact natural-gradient constructions are invariant in principle, but the diagonal approximations that pipelines actually use are among the measurements we audit. Appendix B details what GRR shares with, and where GRR departs from, natural-gradient geometry, quotient geometry, structured pruning, privacy, adapters, and explanation reliability.

We formulate GRR as an operational audit of the identifiability of gradient-derived evidence, built from exact, architecture-native symmetries. Theoretically, we show that same-function reparameterizations can arbitrarily change raw component rankings, characterize the resulting ambiguity, and derive symmetry-aware alternatives, including a quotient-space score that is invariant to any invertible change of basis in the low-rank factors. Empirically, we trace these changes to pruning, clipping, optimizer, and LoRA decisions across encoder, vision, and decoder-only models.

Practitioners may compute gradients with respect to the input, an intermediate activation, a component mask, or a parameter block. The chain rule links these gradients, but each measures sensitivity to a different variable. DP-SGD clips per-example parameter gradients ( Abadi et al., 2016 ) . LLM-Pruner uses weight derivatives to rank parameter groups for pruning ( Ma et al., 2023 ) , and AdaLoRA builds rank-importance scores from parameter–gradient products ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) . GRR therefore focuses on parameter gradients and on gradient-derived measurements and decisions. Pruning also uses derivatives with respect to other variables. Michel et al. (2019) score heads using derivatives with respect to head masks, while Molchanov et al. (2017) score channels using activation–gradient products. These mask and Taylor scores differ from the raw parameter-gradient norms audited below. The same coordinate dependence propagates through iterative pruning, clipped updates, and optimizer-state diagnostics. In the iterative RoBERTa MRPC audit, the final raw top-ablation masks have Jaccard 0.244 0.244 , and the final accuracies differ by 13.48 13.48 percentage points; canonical balancing restores identical schedules. Recomputing gradients at each round carries the coordinate dependence through the pruning schedule. Diagonal empirical-Fisher normalization recovers top-3 overlap 1.0 1.0 in the targeted clipping audit, whereas a transported AdamW state still yields a coordinate-dependent paired-product update. Transferring the optimizer’s history correctly is therefore insufficient to make the update independent of parameter scaling. Exact classifier-factor gauges and six trained LoRA adapters exhibit the same coordinate dependence: Factor-coordinate rankings, clipping decisions, and adapter-compression masks can change while logits are preserved. The raw scores can label different rank coordinates as expendable even when the adapter’s predictions are identical. Same-function coordinate changes can alter pruning, clipping, and update decisions. Appendix D.16 discusses these workflow implications. The failure concerns raw Euclidean measurements and diagnostics that retain coordinate dependence; fixed-function input gradients and invariant scores remain outside the scope of the coordinate-dependence claim. Invariance removes coordinate ambiguity but does not guarantee useful component selection. Appendix F gives the application procedure and acceptance criteria.

Gradient-derived measurements need not be properties of learned functions. GRR makes this distinction operational: The audit rewrites a trained model in two coordinates that provably compute the same function, verifies forward preservation, and tests whether gradient-derived measurements—and the decisions those measurements drive—change. Across Transformer workflows involving encoder and vision classifiers, decoder-only language models, and LoRA adapters, raw Euclidean gradients often change rankings, masks, clipping decisions, and paired-product updates, whereas function-space controls and symmetry-aware normalizations are stable under the scalar gauges tested. Our analysis shows that same-function orbits can realize any raw ranking and unbounded factor-gradient magnitudes, and yields a full- G ​ L ​ ( r ) GL(r) -invariant quotient score. Gradient-based conclusions should therefore be audited under exact same-function reparameterizations or defined directly on quotient-space objects; the audit reduces to a checklist that a practitioner can apply to any new gradient-based diagnostic.

chunks.section: Appendix B Related Work and Distinction
chunks.text: GRR operationalizes the classical coordinate dependence of Euclidean gradients as a decision-facing reliability audit: Fix the learned input–output function, change only the internal coordinate system, verify forward preservation numerically, and test whether a concrete conclusion survives on trained models and downstream decisions. This framing makes GRR closer to a measurement reliability test than to an optimization method.

Reparameterization dependence of Euclidean gradients is classical. Amari (1998) developed natural gradient methods to account for information geometry, Martens and Grosse (2015) make this principle computationally useful for neural networks through Kronecker-factored approximate curvature and related approximations, and Martens (2020) analyzes the sense in which the resulting updates are invariant to smooth reparameterization. The same freedom destabilizes other parameter-space quantities: Sharpness measures and flat-minima claims can be sensitive to reparameterization ( Dinh et al., 2017 ) , loss-surface visualizations require filter-normalized directions before the visualizations are compared ( Li et al., 2018 ) , and scale-invariant networks, path norms, and product norms show that parameter coordinates are not always meaningful ( Neyshabur et al., 2015 ) . Normalization layers make the same freedom concrete: A weight block feeding a batch-normalized ( Ioffe and Szegedy, 2015 ) or weight-normalized ( Salimans and Kingma, 2016 ) unit is positively scale-invariant, so rescaling that block leaves the function untouched while the corresponding gradient norm scales reciprocally ( van Laarhoven, 2017 ) . The Q–K, V–O, and SwiGLU up–down gauges audited here are the paired-projection analogue of that freedom inside a Transformer block.

chunks.section: B.2 Network Symmetry and Quotient Manifolds
chunks.text: Symmetry and gauge freedom in neural networks supply the structural source of these equivalence classes ( Hecht-Nielsen, 1990 ) , and recent surveys emphasize that large same-function parameter orbits are now a central object in overparameterized network theory ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) . Godfrey et al. (2022) catalogue the symmetry groups induced by common activation functions and the action of those groups on internal representations, which is the structural reason one learned function admits many coordinate descriptions. Kunin et al. (2021) show that translation, scale, and rescale symmetries induce exact conservation laws in gradient-flow dynamics, complementary evidence that motion along symmetry directions carries no functional information, whereas Zhao et al. (2022) teleport parameters along a loss level set precisely because that move changes the local gradient. Lim et al. (2024) instead reduce or remove parameter symmetries on the architecture side, while GRR holds the architecture and the learned function fixed and moves along the orbit to test whether a measurement is identifiable.

chunks.section: B.2 Network Symmetry and Quotient Manifolds
chunks.text: Discrete permutation symmetries of hidden units have been used in a different direction, to explain linear mode connectivity between independently trained solutions ( Entezari et al., 2022 ) and to align and merge such solutions in weight space ( Ainsworth et al., 2023 ) . Riemannian quotient geometry for full-rank bilinear factorizations is likewise standard in fixed-rank matrix optimization ( Mishra et al., 2014 ; Absil et al., 2008 ) . Our use of that geometry is measurement-facing, since Theorem 4 , Corollary 6 , Theorem 3 , and Corollary 5 turn factorization freedom into exact attainable sets with clipping and deletion consequences, and Corollary 1 records an invariant fixed-rank product-manifold gradient score.

chunks.section: B.3 Same-Function Coordinates in Deployed Transformer Pipelines
chunks.text: Moving a Transformer along such an orbit is not a hypothetical operation. Data-free quantization equalizes weight ranges across adjacent layers through the scale equivariance of the activation function, which changes coordinates without changing the represented function ( Nagel et al., 2019 ) . Post-training quantization of Transformers applies a mathematically equivalent per-channel rescaling that migrates activation scale into the paired weight matrix ( Xiao et al., 2023 ) , and Ashkboos et al. (2024) use a computational invariance of Transformer blocks to rotate the representation before deleting rows and columns. These pipelines choose a new same-function coordinate for efficiency reasons. GRR tests whether gradient-derived evidence remains stable under such coordinate changes.

GRR complements work on structured pruning and head importance. Michel et al. (2019) study which Transformer heads can be removed without hurting performance, and Voita et al. (2019) find that a small number of specialized heads carries most of the work. Derivative-based importance has a long history in pruning, beginning with the second-order saliency of LeCun et al. (1989) and continuing through first-order gradient and Taylor scores for weights, channels, and structures ( Lee et al., 2019 ; Molchanov et al., 2017 ; Molchanov et al., 2019 ) and jointly learned coupled-structure masks ( Xia et al., 2022 ) . The same kind of evidence now drives structured compression of large language models: Ma et al. (2023) identify structurally coupled parameter groups and rank the groups using gradient-based importance, and Frantar and Alistarh (2023) prune in one shot through layer-wise second-order reconstruction, whereas Sun et al. (2024) deliberately replace gradients by a weight-magnitude and input-activation product. Closest to our concern on the score side, Tanaka et al. (2020) derive conservation laws for synaptic saliency and design a synaptic-flow score whose invariance properties avoid layer collapse. That line designs a score with an invariance in mind. GRR instead tests whether an already-deployed score is identifiable from the learned function. Our one-shot, global, and iterative pruning results show that two same-function coordinates can select different masks and produce different post-pruning validation accuracy or perplexity before any retraining occurs, and the SwiGLU MLP audit extends the same issue to feed-forward channel evidence.

The same distinction applies to privacy-facing, optimizer-state, and adapter uses of gradients. DP-SGD clips per-example gradients before adding noise ( Abadi et al., 2016 ) , recent private-learning systems make clipping more structured through group-wise, per-layer, or adaptive thresholds ( He et al., 2023 ; Xia et al., 2023 ) , and private fine-tuning of large pretrained language models, where the clipping threshold is a tuned and utility-critical hyperparameter, is the workflow our clipping audits target ( Li et al., 2022 ) . Adam ( Kingma and Ba, 2015 ) is explicitly motivated by invariance to diagonal rescaling of the gradients, and AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) builds coordinate-wise state from gradient histories, so that rescaling invariance is a statement about the chosen coordinates rather than about the represented function.

LoRA adds a further identifiability issue because Hu et al. (2022) parameterize an update through factors whose product is used by the forward pass. Recent variants apply factor-specific learning-rate scaling or rank-allocation and pruning signals to those factors ( Hayou et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) . Other work preconditions factor updates with a Riemannian metric ( Zhang and Pilanci, 2024 ) or argues that the factors should be trained differently ( Zhu et al., 2024 ) . The sensitivity-based rank budgeting of Zhang et al. (2023) softly restricts the factor gauge through an orthogonality penalty, an approximate version of the identifiability requirement that Proposition 2 characterizes exactly. GRR does not propose a better clipping rule, optimizer, or rank allocator. The audit instead tests whether the per-example, optimizer-state, and rank-coordinate evidence such workflows consume is identifiable, and our results show that clipping decisions, AdamW paired-product updates, and rank-coordinate importance can all change while the predictions are identical.

The audit is also related to reliability tests for explanations and saliency. Sundararajan et al. (2017) motivate integrated gradients with axioms such as implementation invariance, and Adebayo et al. (2018) show through model-parameter randomization tests that some saliency methods fail basic sanity checks. Closest in spirit, Kindermans et al. (2019) show that some saliency methods are not invariant to a constant input shift that leaves the network output unchanged, an input-side analogue of the parameter-side invariance tested here. Inside Transformers, Jain and Wallace (2019) construct substantially different attention distributions that leave predictions essentially unchanged, so an internal quantity that reads as an explanation need not be pinned down by model behavior, and Wiegreffe and Pinter (2019) qualify that conclusion by showing that the verdict depends on what an explanation is required to do, which is one reason GRR reports a concrete downstream decision instead of an interpretive claim. The same reliability concern extends to training-data attribution, where gradient-based influence estimates are used to explain and debug individual predictions ( Koh and Liang, 2017 ) , are scaled to large language models through curvature approximations ( Grosse et al., 2023 ) , and have also been found fragile in deep non-convex models ( Basu et al., 2021 ) . GRR applies the same reliability philosophy to parameter-gradient evidence, moving along an exact same-function symmetry orbit and testing whether pruning, clipping, or rank-selection conclusions are preserved.

chunks.section: C.1 Grouped-Query Attention and Exactness Conditions
chunks.text: The gauge-invariant objects of a head are therefore the paired products W Q , h ​ W K , h ⊤ W_{Q,h}W_{K,h}^{\top} and W V , h ​ W O , h W_{V,h}W_{O,h} , which are also the combined query–key and value–output maps used in circuit-level descriptions of attention ( Elhage et al., 2021 ) . The individual projection matrices are only one coordinate representation of those maps, so any head-level measurement computed from a single projection factor is a statement about the representation rather than about the head. GQA ( Ainslie et al., 2023 ) restricts the admissible gauges but does not remove those gauges. If m m query heads share one key and value head, exact preservation requires the same scalar c g c_{g} for all query heads in group g g : W Q , h ′ ≔ c g ​ W Q , h , W K , g ′ ≔ c g − 1 ​ W K , g , h ∈ g , W^{\prime}_{Q,h}\coloneqq c_{g}W_{Q,h},\quad W^{\prime}_{K,g}\coloneqq c_{g}^{-1}W_{K,g},\qquad h\in g, (17) and similarly W V , g ′ ≔ c g ​ W V , g W^{\prime}_{V,g}\coloneqq c_{g}W_{V,g} with every output-projection slice for h ∈ g h\in g scaled by c g − 1 c_{g}^{-1} . chunks.section: Further interpretation of the product-manifold score.
chunks.text: The factor-only expression in Eq. 14 is computable without forming Z Z , and Theorem 2 identifies the expression as a Frobenius norm, hence as a nonnegative quantity. Rank-coordinate labels remain basis-dependent under non-diagonal gauges by Corollary 4 . Theorem 2 and Corollary 1 supply a positive counterpart to the non-identifiability results: Whenever the forward loss depends on a full-rank pair only through the product of that pair, whole-product or whole-head first-order evidence can be measured by the fixed-rank product-manifold gradient norm even under non-diagonal mixing. That product-manifold score is the norm of the gradient of ℒ ¯ | ℳ r \overline{\mathcal{L}}|_{\mathcal{M}_{r}} , not in general the ambient norm ∥ Z ∥ F \lVert Z\rVert_{F} : The normal component ( I − Π B ) ​ Z ​ ( I − Π A ) (I-\Pi_{B})Z(I-\Pi_{A}) is invisible to factor gradients. The same r × r r\times r Gram factors P P and Q Q appear in Riemannian preconditioners that accelerate LoRA training ( Zhang and Pilanci, 2024 ) ; here the Gram factors are used to report a gauge-invariant measurement rather than to precondition an update. Separate factor regularization, including untransported weight decay, violates the product-only assumption and must be audited as part of the optimization rule rather than absorbed into these results.

We use function-space ablation as a control for pruning and ablation claims because the ablation targets the same functional intervention. The control costs one forward pass per component or mask, provided that the intervention still denotes the same component after relabeling. Path-normalized scores are a lower-cost screen for reciprocal scalar gauges in Q–K, V–O, and up–down pairs and require only the baseline backward pass, but such scores do not address non-diagonal G ​ L ​ ( r ) GL(r) mixing or gauges that change component identities. Canonical balancing requires no additional gradients and is useful for debugging plots, pruning screens, and LoRA A and B scale audits, but the procedure selects a representative coordinate rather than defining a quotient metric. Diagonal empirical-Fisher normalization targets coordinate-wise scalar scaling and is most practical when per-example gradients are already available; the quality of that normalization depends on damping, sample noise, and neglected off-diagonal structure, and the normalized score does not cover full G ​ L ​ ( r ) GL(r) gauges. The exact quotient-gradient norm in Corollary 1 handles full G ​ L ​ ( r ) GL(r) for identifiable full-rank products at the cost of small Gram-system solves, and that norm yields fixed-rank paired-product tangent rather than rank-coordinate evidence. Paired-product tangents require one backward pass plus product contractions and audit optimizer-step consequences in identifiable products. Finally, a GRR decision audit duplicates the score and downstream decision under a verified same-function transform. The decision audit is therefore the reliability check to run before gradient evidence is treated as functional evidence.

Input gradients of a fixed scalar function stay unchanged wherever the function is differentiable, which is why input-side attributions ( Sundararajan et al., 2017 ) are outside the scope of the coordinate-dependence failure. Exact natural gradients can also be reparameterization-invariant when the metric is transported correctly ( Martens, 2020 ) . For a bilinear product, Theorem 2 recovers the Frobenius norm of the product-manifold gradient from the factor gradients, and Corollary 1 shows that the product-manifold gradient norm is unchanged by any invertible change of factor basis. Taylor and path-normalized scores also stay unchanged under reciprocal scalar rescaling, but this cancellation of reciprocal scale factors does not cover general G ​ L ​ ( r ) GL(r) basis mixing. Appendix C.6 gives the details. Our failure claim concerns raw Euclidean measurements and diagnostics whose approximations retain coordinate dependence.

chunks.section: The function does not determine the raw ranking.
chunks.text: Theorem 1 shows that the same model can have any raw component ranking when only the factor scales change. A component ranked last can become first, and the entire ranking can be reversed, while every prediction stays the same. Every ordering is possible because the components can be rescaled independently and each component’s score has no finite upper bound. The gradients remain valid derivatives in each coordinate system, but raw gradient magnitudes do not establish which components matter to the learned function.

We evaluate on SST-2, MNLI, QNLI, and MRPC from GLUE ( Wang et al., 2019 ) . SST-2 is based on the Stanford Sentiment Treebank ( Socher et al., 2013 ) , MNLI on the Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference corpus ( Williams et al., 2018 ) , and MRPC on the Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus ( Dolan and Brockett, 2005 ) . We use public fine-tuned checkpoints and six independently trained LoRA adapters. For SST-2, we audit all attention layers of DistilBERT ( Sanh et al., 2019 ) and BERT-base ( Devlin et al., 2019 ) , together with selected early, middle, and late layers of ELECTRA-base ( Clark et al., 2020 ) and RoBERTa-base ( Liu et al., 2019 ) , in the main GLUE sweep. For MNLI, QNLI, and MRPC, we audit selected early, middle, and late RoBERTa-base layers. MNLI labels are remapped to the RoBERTa convention of contradiction, neutral, and entailment. GLUE validation accuracy and pruning accuracy use full validation splits. Accuracy differences between decisions made in two same-function coordinates are reported in percentage points, abbreviated pp in tables. Gradient-score audits use 128 validation examples, and per-example clipping audits use 48 examples. To test statistical robustness, we run 324 DistilBERT SST-2 audits over all six layers, shuffled validation subsets of size 32, 128, and 256, three shuffled seeds, Q–K and V–O pairs, and mild, medium, and aggressive gauge ranges. We run all-layer 96-audit checks for BERT-base, ELECTRA-base, and RoBERTa on SST-2, as well as RoBERTa on MNLI, QNLI, and MRPC, with subset size 128, two shuffled seeds, Q–K and V–O pairs, and mild and aggressive gauge ranges.

Because clipping decisions are especially sensitive to audit-set size, a separate 216-audit DistilBERT on SST-2 clipping robustness suite covers all six layers, 48- and 128-example shuffled subsets, three shuffled seeds, Q–K and V–O pairs, and mild, medium, and aggressive gauge ranges. A 256-example clipping holdout covers early, middle, and late DistilBERT layers, a held-out seed, both attention pairs, and all three gauge ranges. Appendix E records the exact seed value used by each suite. As a cross-domain check, we also audit all 12 layers of a ViT-base checkpoint fine-tuned on CIFAR-10 ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2021 ; Krizhevsky et al., 2009 ) , using the Hugging Face identifier nateraw/vit-base-patch16-224-cifar10 . We evaluate accuracy and pruning effects on the full 10,000-image CIFAR-10 test split, compute gradients on 256 test images, and compute per-example clipping on 48 images. The ViT experiment is reported separately from the GLUE aggregate because the modality differs. To test whether the phenomenon extends beyond encoder classification, we audit decoder-only next-token language modeling on WikiText-2 ( Merity et al., 2017 ) . We use GPT-2-medium and GPT-2-large ( Radford et al., 2019 ) and a Llama-style ( Touvron et al., 2023 ) GQA model, TinyLlama/TinyLlama-1.1B-intermediate-step-1431k-3T ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) . For GPT-2-medium, we audit all 24 layers, evaluate perplexity on 128 contiguous 128-token test blocks, compute gradients on 32 validation blocks, and compute per-sequence clipping on 16 validation blocks. A GPT-2-medium global V–O pruning profile covers all 384 heads with mild, medium, and aggressive gauges, a 15% global head budget, the same 128 test blocks, and 32 validation audit blocks.

The remaining decoder-only audits follow the same structure at smaller evaluation budgets. For GPT-2-large, we audit all 36 layers with 64 test blocks, 16 validation audit blocks, and eight per-sequence clipping blocks, together with a global V–O pruning profile over all 720 heads under the same profile family and a 15% budget. For TinyLlama, we audit all 22 attention layers with 64 test blocks, eight validation audit blocks, and eight per-sequence clipping blocks; the 32 TinyLlama query heads share four key and value heads, so the audit uses the group-wise gauge described above. We also audit the TinyLlama SwiGLU MLP up–down symmetry on layers 0, 11, and 21 using the same WikiText-2 blocks and top-128 channel rankings over all 5,632 intermediate channels. Because exact forward preservation is the audit precondition, the experiment drivers disable TF32 matrix multiplication and use FP32 matmuls for the preservation checks. The experiment code is organized as a single audit suite. Separate drivers run the main GLUE audit, the trained LoRA audits and rank-pruning recovery curves, the subset and scale robustness suite, the clipping robustness suite, the ViT layer-level audit, the ViT full-test global-pruning calibration, the decoder-only WikiText-2 attention, global-pruning, and MLP audits, the one-shot and iterative pruning pipelines, profile-wise global-pruning scale calibrations for RoBERTa on SST-2, QNLI, and MRPC, the downstream-remedy audit, the AdamW optimizer-state audit, the checkpoint-scale audit, and the training-time imbalance calibration.

A multi-GPU suite runner can execute these drivers as independent GPU-isolated shards and merge the shard outputs into a single result table, while a validation script checks the reported invariants: baseline quality, forward-preservation tolerances for logit drift and prediction and argmax flip rates, finite numeric fields, unique result keys, and expected evidence rows including the ViT and cross-task global-pruning profiles. A lightweight summarization script reconstructs the reported aggregates directly from that result table. The runs were executed on a 4 × \times H100 node; each audit uses deterministic seeds and records the exact model tag, task, transform, metric, and sample count in the table. chunks.text: Every experiment begins from numerically verified same-function coordinates. The layer-level audits test score, ranking, clipping, and downstream-decision stability; the global and iterative pruning and LoRA studies test complete workflows. The ViT, decoder-only, GQA, and SwiGLU audits extend the same protocol across modalities and architectures, while checkpoint-scale and training-time measurements calibrate the stress-test gauges against naturally occurring imbalance. Function-space ablation, path normalization, canonical balancing, diagonal Fisher normalization, and the ViT input-pixel gradient serve as controls for the symmetries or coordinate systems each control targets. chunks.section: D.2 Audit Roadmap and Workflow Configuration
chunks.text: The robustness sweeps and experiments with other numbers of heads, shared groups, or channels use geometric spacing over the applicable mild [ 0.5 , 2.0 ] [0.5,2.0] , medium [ 0.25 , 4.0 ] [0.25,4.0] , or aggressive [ 0.125 , 10.0 ] [0.125,10.0] range. The 12-head global-profile driver uses the same 12-head scale vector for the aggressive case. For classifier factors, we use both diagonal gauges and non-diagonal G ​ L ​ ( r ) GL(r) gauges. For the trained LoRA adapters, we train DistilBERT-base on SST-2 for 3 epochs under three training seeds with rank 16, α = 32 \alpha=32 , dropout 0.05, AdamW, linear warmup, and LoRA modules on the Q, K, V, and O projections. We also train rank-8 RoBERTa adapters on MRPC from the public textattack/roberta-base-MRPC checkpoint with α = 16 \alpha=16 , the same three seeds, LoRA modules on the Q, K, and V projections, and the classifier saved with the adapter. As a more pipeline-like pruning check, we run four rounds of iterative global V–O pruning or top-head ablation with RoBERTa on MRPC. Each round recomputes raw gradients on the current masked model, selects seven additional heads out of 144, zeros the output paths of those heads, and evaluates on the full validation split. The original, reparameterized, and canonically balanced runs start from same-function coordinates and use the same audit subset.

chunks.section: D.2 Audit Roadmap and Workflow Configuration
chunks.text: For LoRA rank-pruning recovery, each seed uses the bottom-25% rank coordinates selected by the original and reparameterized raw rank-gradient scores. Both selected rank sets are applied to the same original trained adapter, pruned LoRA ranks are kept zero by masking A rows and B columns, and the remaining trainable adapter and classifier parameters are recovered for 2 epochs. DistilBERT on SST-2 uses the full SST-2 train split with AdamW, learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} , warmup ratio 0.06, weight decay 0.01, batch size 64, and gradient clipping at 1.0. RoBERTa on MRPC uses the full MRPC train split with learning rate 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} and batch size 32, matching the smaller task. Finally, profile-wise global V–O pruning calibrations cover RoBERTa on SST-2, QNLI, and MRPC, ViT on CIFAR-10, and GPT-2-medium and GPT-2-large on WikiText-2. The GLUE global-pruning calibrations use the full validation split for each task, the ViT global calibration uses the full 10,000-image CIFAR-10 test split, and the GPT-2 global calibrations use 128 contiguous WikiText-2 test blocks for GPT-2-medium and 64 blocks for GPT-2-large. All use mild, medium, and aggressive same-function V–O gauge profiles and fixed audit subsets for gradients.

chunks.section: D.2 Audit Roadmap and Workflow Configuration
chunks.text: The remaining audits are a ViT input-pixel gradient control, a targeted downstream-remedy audit on the layer-11 V–O pair of RoBERTa on MRPC, an AdamW optimizer-state audit, a checkpoint-scale audit, and a training-time imbalance calibration. The ViT input-gradient control applies the same three global V–O profiles and compares supervised-loss gradients with respect to normalized input pixels on 32 CIFAR-10 test images, after freezing parameter-gradient storage. The downstream-remedy audit estimates diagonal empirical-Fisher scores from 64 per-example validation gradients and computes a clipped paired-product tangent in the style of differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD), using the original median target-pair norm as clipping threshold. The AdamW optimizer-state audit accumulates first and second moments over 512 MRPC training examples without changing parameters, compares directly accumulated transformed moments to moments transported from the original coordinate, and then compares the one-step AdamW paired-product tangent. The checkpoint-scale audit measures the natural per-head Q–K and V–O paired norm imbalance in the eight public encoder and ViT checkpoints used above. The training-time imbalance calibration fine-tunes distilbert-base-uncased on the full SST-2 train split for 3 epochs with AdamW and records all-layer paired norm imbalance after each epoch. These calibrations quantify the mild same-function scale variation already present in trained checkpoints and in a standard full-model fine-tuning run.

We evaluate six trained LoRA adapters in two settings that vary the dataset, base model, and rank budget. Three rank-16 DistilBERT adapters are trained on SST-2 for three epochs with three seeds, yielding mean validation accuracy 89.87 % 89.87\% across runs that range from 89.68 % 89.68\% to 90.25 % 90.25\% . Three rank-8 RoBERTa adapters are trained on MRPC from textattack/roberta-base-MRPC for three epochs, yielding mean accuracy 90.28 % 90.28\% across runs that range from 89.95 % 89.95\% to 90.69 % 90.69\% . We audit all LoRA A and B factors in the attention projections: 384 rank coordinates per DistilBERT seed and 288 per RoBERTa seed. Exact diagonal LoRA gauges produce no prediction flips; maximum logit differences are 5.25 × 10 − 6 5.25\times 10^{-6} and 2.13 × 10 − 5 2.13\times 10^{-5} , respectively. For DistilBERT on SST-2, raw rank-gradient top-12 overlap has median 0.417 0.417 and paired-product tangent top-12 overlap has median 0.250 0.250 , with median tangent ratio 5.25 5.25 . For rank-8 RoBERTa on MRPC, the corresponding medians are 0.333 0.333 , 0.250 0.250 , and 5.08 5.08 . The same dependence changes adapter-compression masks. Section D.6 and Table 6 report the rank-pruning, ablation, and recovery results.

chunks.section: D.6 Trained LoRA Adapter Compression and Recovery
chunks.text: The coordinate dependence also changes adapter-compression decisions. Pruning the bottom 25% of LoRA rank coordinates by raw rank-gradient score gives median rank-set Jaccard 0.401 0.401 for DistilBERT on SST-2 and 0.455 0.455 for RoBERTa on MRPC. Top-25% ablation gives median Jaccard 0.297 0.297 and 0.500 0.500 , respectively. Accuracy gaps are smaller than the rank-set disagreement: Median bottom-pruning gaps are 0.34 0.34 percentage points for SST-2 and 0.00 0.00 for MRPC, while median top-ablation gaps are 1.03 1.03 and 0.25 0.25 percentage points. The rank identities selected by raw gradient evidence are therefore not functionally identifiable, even when validation accuracy is partially buffered. We then run rank-pruning recovery curves for the bottom-25% masks. Both masks are applied to the same original trained adapter, so the two runs differ only in the rank sets selected by the original and reparameterized gradient scores. After two recovery epochs, the median coordinate-induced gap is 0.23 0.23 percentage points for SST-2 and 0.00 0.00 for MRPC; the maximum MRPC gap is 0.49 0.49 percentage points. Recovery can absorb part of the utility loss, but recovery does not make the selected rank sets agree. Thus PEFT compression analyses based on raw factor-gradient rank coordinates should be audited or expressed through product-space quantities. chunks.text: The aggressive gauges above are deliberately adversarial stress tests. To calibrate the gauge scale, we also measure the paired projection norms already present in the eight public encoder and ViT checkpoints in Table 4 . Let N left , h N_{\mathrm{left},h} and N right , h N_{\mathrm{right},h} be the Euclidean norms of the complete branch parameter blocks that are actually rescaled: the relevant weight slice together with the corresponding Q, K, or V projection bias when present, while an unchanged output-projection bias is excluded. For each head, we report r h ≔ max ⁡ { N left , h N right , h , N right , h N left , h } , r_{h}\coloneqq\max\left\{\frac{N_{\mathrm{left},h}}{N_{\mathrm{right},h}},\frac{N_{\mathrm{right},h}}{N_{\mathrm{left},h}}\right\}, (82) where the two branches form either a Q–K pair or a V–O pair. The canonical scalar needed to equalize the pair is s h ≔ N right , h / N left , h s_{h}\coloneqq\sqrt{N_{\mathrm{right},h}/N_{\mathrm{left},h}} .

The trained checkpoints already contain mild norm imbalance, especially in V–O pairs, but not the aggressive scales used for worst-case GRR stress tests. Across the eight checkpoints, the mean checkpoint-level Q–K median is r h = 1.023 r_{h}=1.023 , the mean checkpoint-level 90th percentile is 1.063 1.063 , and the largest observed value is 1.187 1.187 ; no Q–K head exceeds 1.25 1.25 , and the required balancing scales stay within [ 0.918 , 1.055 ] [0.918,1.055] . For V–O, the corresponding checkpoint-summary means and largest observed value are 1.093 1.093 , 1.170 1.170 , and 1.429 1.429 ; the checkpoint-level fraction above 1.25 1.25 is 5.2 % 5.2\% on average and at most 10.4 % 10.4\% , with balancing scales in [ 0.837 , 1.077 ] [0.837,1.077] . Thus the mild robustness suite is closest to natural checkpoint-scale variation, while medium and aggressive gauges test whether a measurement is identifiable on the full same-function orbit. This mild norm imbalance is consistent with the conservation-law perspective: For homogeneous factor pairs, gradient flow conserves the difference of squared branch norms, so training does not push a pair far apart when initialization uses small balanced weights ( Du et al., 2018 ) . That argument constrains where optimization travels, not the orbit on which a measurement has to be identifiable.

We also fine-tune distilbert-base-uncased on the full SST-2 train split for 3 epochs with AdamW at learning rate 2 × 10 − 5 2\times 10^{-5} , tracking the same statistic throughout training. The reproducibility details give the complete recipe. Validation accuracy over epochs 0 through 3 is 50.92 % 50.92\% , 90.37 % 90.37\% , 90.71 % 90.71\% , and 90.48 % 90.48\% , respectively, ending at a level comparable to the public DistilBERT checkpoint used in the main audit. Across all 72 attention heads, however, the imbalance summary is unchanged to three decimal places: Q–K has median 1.015 1.015 and maximum 1.187 1.187 , V–O has median 1.049 1.049 and maximum 1.122 1.122 , and no head exceeds 1.25 1.25 . Paired norm imbalance therefore remains mild throughout standard fine-tuning.

We run the same attention-pair audit on ViT-base fine-tuned on CIFAR-10 to test whether the failure crosses modalities. The checkpoint obtains 98.51 % 98.51\% accuracy on the full 10,000-image test split, as recorded in Table 4 . Across all 12 layers and both Q–K and V–O gauges, prediction flips remain zero. Raw head-gradient top-3 overlap ranges from 0 0 to 1 1 with median 1 / 3 1/3 . The corresponding mean ratio ranges from 2.59 2.59 to 3.84 3.84 with median 3.02 3.02 . Paired-product tangent overlap also ranges from 0 0 to 1 1 with median 1 / 3 1/3 . The tangent mean ratio ranges from 11.58 11.58 to 27.22 27.22 with median 17.91 17.91 . Per-example clipping flip rates range from 47.9 % 47.9\% to 50.0 % 50.0\% with median 50.0 % 50.0\% . The remedies behave as expected. Path-normalized gradients have top-3 overlap 1.000 1.000 and mean ratio 1.00 1.00 , both with degenerate ranges at those values. Function-space head ablation and canonically balanced gradient scores likewise have top-3 overlap 1.000 1.000 in all 24 audits and mean ratios approximately 1 1 . Raw top-3 ablation decisions, by contrast, have median Jaccard 0.2 0.2 and yield an accuracy gap of 2.8 2.8 percentage points on the full CIFAR-10 test split. The same symmetry-driven measurement failure therefore appears outside text encoders. We also run a full-test global V–O pruning calibration on the same ViT checkpoint. The setup mirrors the RoBERTa global-profile audits: For each mild, medium, and aggressive same-function V–O profile, we compute one global raw-gradient ranking over all 144 heads using a 256-image audit subset, prune or ablate 22 heads, and evaluate the resulting mask on the full 10,000-image CIFAR-10 test split.

Table 10 shows that the decision-level failure is not confined to text models. Mild gauges already change the top-ablation mask, with Jaccard 0.517 0.517 and a full-test accuracy gap of 4.35 4.35 percentage points. Bottom pruning is less destructive but still changes masks and produces a gap of up to 7.02 7.02 percentage points. Canonical balancing restores identical global masks and zero accuracy gaps for all three profiles. As a boundary control, we also test a quantity that should be a property of the fixed input–output function: the gradient of the supervised loss with respect to normalized input pixels. We apply the same global V–O profiles to all ViT attention layers and compare input-pixel gradients on 32 CIFAR-10 test images. The control delimits the claim precisely: The failure concerns parameter and internal gradient-derived measurements, not exact input-space derivatives of a preserved scalar function.

We next audit decoder-only next-token prediction on WikiText-2. This decoder-only setting differs from GLUE in architecture, objective, output space, and decision metric. The loss is token-level cross-entropy, pruning is evaluated by perplexity, and the TinyLlama audit includes GQA with only four key and value heads shared by 32 query heads. Across all 24 layers of GPT-2-medium, all 36 layers of GPT-2-large, and all 22 layers of TinyLlama, with both Q–K and V–O gauges, the median next-token argmax flip rate is zero. GPT-2-medium and TinyLlama have zero flips in all audits. GPT-2-large has one finite-precision layer-9 Q–K case with flip rate 0.0492 % 0.0492\% and maximum logit difference 9.54 × 10 − 5 9.54\times 10^{-5} . Raw gradient evidence is again unstable, as Table 11 summarizes. GPT-2-medium raw head-gradient and paired-product tangent top-3 overlap both have median 1 / 3 1/3 , with zero-overlap failures. GPT-2-large shows the same medians over all 36 layers, with tangent overlap ranging from 0 0 to 2 / 3 2/3 . TinyLlama has higher raw-gradient overlap, with median 1 / 2 1/2 , but the TinyLlama paired-product tangent overlap has median 0 0 ; the tangent mean ratio has median 23.26 × 23.26\times and ranges from 12.37 × 12.37\times to 40.89 × 40.89\times . Per-sequence clipping decisions flip for 50.0 % 50.0\% of audited sequences in every decoder-only run. Function-space head ablation remains invariant, with top-3 overlap 1.0 1.0 in all 164 audits.

The layer-local pruning check is decision-facing as well. Raw bottom-3 head-pruning masks have Jaccard median 0.2 0.2 for GPT-2-medium and GPT-2-large and median 0 0 for TinyLlama. Thus the same reliability failure appears in generative decoder-only models, including a GQA Llama-style architecture. chunks.section: D.11 Llama-Style SwiGLU MLP Channel Audit
chunks.text: To test feed-forward channels, we audit TinyLlama SwiGLU up–down gauges at layers 0, 11, and 21, each with 5,632 channels. We use scales from 0.125 0.125 to 10.0 10.0 , top-128 rankings on eight WikiText-2 blocks, and gradients restricted to each pair. Predictions never flip. Across layers, raw channel-gradient top-128 overlap ranges from 0.344 0.344 to 0.422 0.422 with median 0.352 0.352 . The mean ratio ranges from 2.45 2.45 to 2.62 2.62 with median 2.55 2.55 . Paired-product tangent overlap ranges from 0.211 0.211 to 0.242 0.242 with median 0.234 0.234 . The tangent mean ratio ranges from 9.84 × 9.84\times to 13.06 × 13.06\times with median 12.67 × 12.67\times . Per-sequence clipping decisions flip for 50.0 % 50.0\% of audited sequences. Canonical balancing makes both overlaps and ratios 1.00 1.00 throughout, showing that the failure extends beyond attention.

One-shot pruning can understate the workflow consequence because practical pipelines often recompute scores after each masking step. We therefore run an iterative V–O schedule with RoBERTa on MRPC. Starting from original and reparameterized coordinates with identical validation predictions, each round recomputes global raw-gradient scores, selects seven additional heads, and accumulates the mask for four rounds. The final mask prunes 28 of 144 heads, or 19.4 % 19.4\% . For the remedy check, we canonically balance both same-function coordinates before running the same iterative schedule. Figure 5 shows that same-function coordinate choice changes the entire schedule. Under bottom pruning, the final raw masks have Jaccard 0.191 0.191 even though the accuracy curves remain close: The maximum gap is 1.96 1.96 percentage points, and the final accuracies are 89.22 % 89.22\% and 89.95 % 89.95\% in the original and reparameterized coordinates, respectively. Under top-head ablation, the final raw masks have Jaccard 0.244 0.244 and the curves separate: The largest validation gap is 18.14 18.14 percentage points, and the final accuracies are 68.63 % 68.63\% and 82.11 % 82.11\% in the original and reparameterized coordinates, respectively, a gap of 13.48 13.48 percentage points. Canonical balancing removes the schedule discrepancy for the V–O scalar gauge: Final Jaccard is 1.000 1.000 for both decisions, with zero coordinate-induced accuracy gap and final accuracies of 88.24 % 88.24\% in both bottom-pruning runs and 68.63 % 68.63\% in both top-ablation runs. Thus GRR identifies instability in an iterative decision pipeline that repeatedly consumes gradient evidence.

Figure 5: Iterative pruning schedules for RoBERTa on MRPC. The right plot shows that raw same-function reparameterization changes the accumulated masks, and the center plot shows that the same reparameterization also changes the accuracy trajectory under top-head ablation. Canonical balancing maps both coordinates to the same schedule for the V–O scalar gauge, so the balanced curve tracks the original coordinate and the final mask Jaccard is 1.000 1.000 .

The targeted layer-11 V–O audit for RoBERTa on MRPC has zero forward prediction flips on the 128-example audit subset, yet the raw Euclidean head-gradient score again fails: Spearman correlation is negative, top-3 overlap is 1 / 3 1/3 , and the mean score ratio is 2.92 2.92 . Diagonal empirical-Fisher normalization is much more stable, with top-3 overlap 1.0 1.0 , Spearman 0.965 0.965 , and mean ratio 0.982 0.982 . This stability of the Fisher-normalized score is consistent with the expected cancellation of scalar-gauge factors in the normalized score. Gauge balancing gives a similar top-3 recovery for the V–O scalar gauge.

The same audit also measures a DP-SGD-style clipped update. Using the original median target-pair gradient norm as clipping threshold, 50.0 % 50.0\% of per-example clipping decisions flip after the same-function gauge. More importantly, the paired-product tangent induced by the clipped raw update is not just rescaled: The tangent’s cosine similarity with the original-coordinate update is 0.425 0.425 , the relative ℓ 2 \ell_{2} difference is 10.90 10.90 , and the norm ratio is 11.29 11.29 . This comparison of clipped paired-product tangents links the clipping decision flips to an update-level consequence.

The clipped-update result raises the related issue of whether consistent transport of AdamW moments across the same-function gauge makes the update a function-level object. We test the effect of transporting AdamW moments directly on the same layer-11 V–O pair of RoBERTa on MRPC. We accumulate AdamW first and second moments over 512 MRPC training examples without changing parameters. In the reparameterized coordinate, these directly accumulated moments match the original moments transported by the scalar gradient transformation: The relative ℓ 2 \ell_{2} errors are 4.48 × 10 − 7 4.48\times 10^{-7} for the first moment and 2.94 × 10 − 7 2.94\times 10^{-7} for the second. Thus the audit is not merely detecting a missing state transport. Even with the transported AdamW moments, the paired-product tangent induced by one AdamW update is still coordinate-dependent. For both the directly accumulated transformed state and the transported original state, the update has cosine similarity 0.676 0.676 with the original-coordinate product update, relative ℓ 2 \ell_{2} difference 2.934 2.934 , and norm ratio 3.515 3.515 . Canonical V–O balancing is much closer to the original update, with cosine similarity 0.995 0.995 , relative ℓ 2 \ell_{2} difference 0.107 0.107 , and norm ratio 1.013 1.013 . This optimizer-state audit separates two issues: Adam moments can be moved consistently as coordinate statistics, but the usual coordinate-wise AdamW step does not induce an invariant paired-product update under the audited gauge.

chunks.section: Coordinate choices change pruning, clipping, and updates.
chunks.text: Changing parameter coordinates affects four common uses of parameter gradients. In structured compression, raw scores can select different head and channel masks for the same unpruned model. In our largest GLUE global-pruning case, replacing four selected heads creates an accuracy gap of 43.92 43.92 percentage points. The disagreement also persists through repeated decisions: After four rounds of top-head ablation on RoBERTa MRPC, the final masks have Jaccard 0.244 0.244 and the accuracy gap is 13.48 13.48 percentage points. In private training, a median 20.8 % 20.8\% of examples change clipping status under a same-function gauge. The privacy accounting is unchanged, but the set of clipped per-example gradients and the resulting clipping bias depend on the coordinates. Adapter workflows use factor gradients to allocate and prune rank budgets; the resulting rank-coordinate importance is basis-dependent unless defined through the product or a fixed gauge. Even a correctly transported AdamW state yields a coordinate-dependent paired-product update, so adaptive preconditioning alone does not remove the dependence. Each workflow therefore needs to check whether the pruning, clipping, rank-allocation, or update decisions remain unchanged when only the parameter coordinates change.

All reported numbers are generated by the Python audit drivers and serialized to a single result table. Each row is keyed by experiment , quantity , method , transform , and metric ; the remaining columns are value , baseline , transformed , forward_max_abs_delta , n , and note . A companion run-details record stores model tags, seeds, gauge scales, and selected heads or ranks. The full audit suite is executed in one pass by the suite runner under the full profile with all four GPUs visible and four concurrent shards. Separate entry points then regenerate the figure panels from the result table, export the table mapping, export the reproducibility manifest, validate the results, and print the reported aggregates. The suite runner executes independent shards with one visible GPU per process and merges the per-shard result tables by replacing matching experiment names. Individual drivers also replace the rows and detail entries for the corresponding experiment family before appending new results, so rerunning one shard does not leave duplicate keys or discard unrelated completed audits. The merger checks for duplicate result keys, sorts rows by the result key, and atomically replaces the result and detail artifacts after all bytes have been written, making the reported tables insensitive to GPU completion order and interrupted writes. The runner writes one log per shard, treats a successful process that failed to write the expected result and detail artifacts as an error, and includes the tail of the shard log in failure messages.

The validation code checks finite numeric fields, unique result keys, baseline-quality thresholds, forward-preservation tolerances, required evidence rows for GLUE, ViT, decoder-only language modeling, global pruning, clipping robustness, AdamW optimizer-state auditing, training-time imbalance, and LoRA, representative reported values, and the expected figure and table-mapping artifacts. The baseline thresholds are set to reject weak checkpoints: For example, RoBERTa and ELECTRA on SST-2 must exceed 93 % 93\% and 94 % 94\% validation accuracy, respectively, ViT on CIFAR-10 must exceed 98 % 98\% test accuracy, and GPT-2 and TinyLlama WikiText-2 perplexities must remain below the stated limits. The artifact and hash checks are separate from the numeric checks, so result validation and reproducibility-artifact validation can be inspected independently.

The reported aggregates and figure panels are regenerated from the serialized result table. A declarative mapping associates every reported table or result family with the corresponding experiment filter, quantities, metrics, and representative value; an exporter then recomputes that mapping directly from the result table. The companion mapping artifact therefore provides the exact row-level trace from each reported result to the corresponding underlying records without requiring readers to search experiment logs. We also export a reproducibility manifest. The manifest records SHA-256 hashes and sizes for the result table, the run-details record, the table mapping, and the generated figure PDFs. The manifest also records hashes for the experiment source files, package versions for PyTorch, Transformers, Datasets, PEFT, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, scikit-learn, Matplotlib, and Hugging Face Hub, CUDA and GPU metadata including the NVIDIA driver when nvidia-smi is available, the configured cache directories, git commit and dirty-state metadata, cached Hugging Face model snapshot hashes, and Hugging Face Datasets builder-cache fingerprints. For datasets, the manifest records the local cache directory, configuration, version, builder hash, dataset_info.json SHA-256 hash, and split shard sizes. Model and dataset revisions are not forced in the drivers. The manifest therefore records the cached local resource fingerprints to make the exact resources auditable. The validation script checks that the manifest hashes match the current result artifacts and experiment source files, so a result table or driver change cannot silently drift from the recorded reproducibility metadata.

GLUE validation accuracy and pruning accuracy use full validation splits for SST-2, QNLI, and MRPC and validation_matched for MNLI. CIFAR-10 accuracy and pruning effects use the full public test split. WikiText-2 language-modeling perplexity uses contiguous 128-token blocks from the public test split. Gradient audits use deterministic prefixes or shuffled subsets with recorded seeds; robustness audits vary subset size and seed explicitly.

The main text reports how many seeds each suite uses; the exact values are the following. The 324-audit DistilBERT robustness suite and the 216-audit clipping robustness suite both shuffle the validation subsets with seeds 7, 11, and 13, and the all-layer 96-audit breadth checks use seeds 7 and 11. The 256-example clipping holdout uses seed 17, which no other robustness suite uses, so that suite is a genuine holdout in both subset size and seed. The six trained LoRA adapters use training seeds 7, 11, and 13 for both the rank-16 DistilBERT group on SST-2 and the rank-8 RoBERTa group on MRPC, and each LoRA rank-pruning recovery run inherits the seed of the source adapter. Audits that consume deterministic validation prefixes rather than shuffled subsets, including the main GLUE layer sweep, the ViT audits, and the decoder-only WikiText-2 audits, do not depend on a seed choice. The seed of every recorded run is stored together with the model tag and gauge scales in the run-details record.

The main classifiers and ViT are public fine-tuned checkpoints. The LoRA experiments train DistilBERT-base on SST-2 for 3 epochs with rank 16, α = 32 \alpha=32 , dropout 0.05, AdamW, learning rate 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} , weight decay 0.01, linear warmup ratio 0.06, batch size 64, and gradient clipping at 1.0. The RoBERTa LoRA experiments on MRPC start from textattack/roberta-base-MRPC and train rank-8 adapters for 3 epochs with α = 16 \alpha=16 , AdamW, learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} , weight decay 0.01, linear warmup ratio 0.06, batch size 32, Q, K, and V target modules, and the classifier saved with the adapter. LoRA rank-pruning recovery keeps the selected rank coordinates zero and fine-tunes the remaining trainable adapter and classifier parameters for 2 epochs: SST-2 uses learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} and batch size 64, while MRPC uses learning rate 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} and batch size 32. The training-time imbalance calibration fine-tunes all parameters of distilbert-base-uncased on the full SST-2 train split for 3 epochs with AdamW, learning rate 2 × 10 − 5 2\times 10^{-5} , weight decay 0.01, linear warmup ratio 0.06, batch size 64, and gradient clipping at 1.0; validation accuracy reaches 90.71 % 90.71\% after epoch 2.

The AdamW optimizer-state audit uses the same layer-11 V–O pair of RoBERTa on MRPC, accumulates β 1 = 0.9 , β 2 = 0.999 \beta_{1}=0.9,\beta_{2}=0.999 moments over 512 MRPC train examples in 16-example batches without optimizer steps, and compares the one-step AdamW paired-product tangent with ϵ = 10 − 8 \epsilon=10^{-8} and weight decay 0.01. The iterative pruning audit uses the RoBERTa checkpoint on MRPC, a 128-example validation audit subset for gradient recomputation, the full 408-example validation split for accuracy, four rounds, and seven newly selected global V–O heads per round.

The GLUE profile-wise global-pruning calibrations use RoBERTa checkpoints on SST-2, QNLI, and MRPC, full validation splits, a 128-example audit subset, global V–O decisions for bottom-15% pruning and top-15% ablation, and mild, medium, and aggressive gauge profiles. The ViT global-pruning calibration uses nateraw/vit-base-patch16-224-cifar10 , a 256-image test audit subset for gradients, the full 10,000-image CIFAR-10 test split for accuracy, the same 15% global V–O head budget, and the same three gauge profiles. The ViT input-gradient control uses the same checkpoint, 32 CIFAR-10 test images, global V–O gauges at mild, medium, and aggressive scales, and gradients of the supervised loss with respect to normalized input pixels. The GPT-2-medium global-pruning calibration uses all 384 attention heads, 32 WikiText-2 validation audit blocks for gradients, 128 WikiText-2 test blocks for perplexity, the same 15% global V–O head budget, and the same three gauge profiles. The SwiGLU MLP audit uses the TinyLlama checkpoint, layers 0, 11, and 21, eight 128-token validation blocks for gradient scoring, eight one-sequence blocks for clipping decisions, top-128 channel rankings, and gradients restricted to the audited up–down projection pair. The GPT-2-large global V–O profile reported in Table 12 uses all 720 attention heads, 16 WikiText-2 validation audit blocks for gradients, 64 WikiText-2 test blocks for perplexity, batch size 2, the same 15% global head budget, and the same mild, medium, and aggressive gauge profiles as the GPT-2-medium calibration.

The reported run was executed on a 4 × \times NVIDIA H100 node with about 96GB memory per GPU. The suite runner assigns one shard process per visible GPU and uses four concurrent GPU-isolated shards. The largest single-GPU shards are the TinyLlama attention and MLP audits and the GPT-2-large global pruning profile; the configured block counts and batch sizes fit on one H100. With warm Hugging Face caches, the full suite completes as an overnight multi-GPU job. For forward-preservation checks, TF32 matrix multiplication is disabled and FP32 matmuls are used to avoid conflating finite-precision kernel differences with symmetry failure.

chunks.section: Appendix F A GRR Checklist for New Gradient-Based Diagnostics
chunks.text: The following procedure produces the GRR report of Definition 1 for a diagnostic that was not studied here. Appendix C.2 gives an executable version for the attention case, and the settings quoted below match the settings used throughout our experiments.

To apply GRR, first identify a parameter transformation that preserves the model’s input–output function exactly. Apply the transformation at several scales, from mild rescaling to a stronger stress test, and verify that logits and predictions remain unchanged within numerical tolerance. Reject runs that fail this forward check before comparing gradients. Then compare both the gradient-based scores and the pruning, clipping, or rank-selection decisions those scores produce. Repeat the comparison with a control that is invariant to the tested transformation, using a function-space score for the same intervention or a quotient-space score for a bilinear product. If the function is unchanged but the workflow selects different heads, examples, or rank coordinates, the decision depends on the parameter representation and should not be presented as a property of the learned function. The checklist below gives the recommended gauge profiles and acceptance criteria.

chunks.section: Exact symmetry of the audited architecture.
chunks.text: Standard multi-head attention admits head-wise Q–K and V–O scalar gauges, SwiGLU blocks admit up–down channel gauges, and low-rank adapters admit the full G ​ L ​ ( r ) GL(r) factor gauge. Under RoPE, only the scalar part of the Q–K gauge survives; under GQA, the gauge acts on shared key–value groups rather than on individual query heads. Verify exactness symbolically before running anything, since an approximate symmetry converts every later comparison into a confound. If the audited component admits no exact symmetry, report the absence of an exact symmetry as an informative result about identifiability and stop.

We recommend three gauge profiles. A mild profile spanning [ 0.5 , 2.0 ] [0.5,2.0] brackets the paired-norm imbalance already present in public checkpoints, which the checkpoint-scale audit in Appendix D places within balancing scales [ 0.837 , 1.077 ] [0.837,1.077] . A medium profile spans [ 0.25 , 4.0 ] [0.25,4.0] . An aggressive profile spanning [ 0.125 , 10.0 ] [0.125,10.0] probes identifiability on the full orbit. Reporting only the aggressive profile invites the objection that the gauge is artificial, whereas reporting only the mild profile understates how badly the measurement is underdetermined.

Report the maximum logit difference δ f ​ ( T ) \delta_{f}(T) and the prediction flip rate on the audit set. Discard any run whose flips are not attributable to finite precision; in our audits the classification flip rate is zero throughout, and the only nonzero decoder-only case is a finite-precision GPT-2-large flip rate of 0.0492 % 0.0492\% . A run that fails the forward-preservation gate describes a broken transformation rather than an unreliable diagnostic, and reporting such a run as a GRR failure is an error.

Report the rank correlation ρ R \rho_{R} , the top- k k overlap O k O_{k} at the k k that the workflow actually uses, and the ratio of mean scores. A mean ratio far from one indicates that any absolute threshold placed on the score, such as a clipping threshold or a pruning cutoff, is gauge-dependent even when the induced ordering happens to survive.

This decision-level comparison is the step that carries the claim. Report the agreement of the selected sets, for instance the Jaccard index of two pruning masks, together with the gap in the metric the workflow optimizes. A stable score with an unstable decision and a stable decision with an unstable score are both possible, and only the decision-level comparison states what is at stake for a practitioner. Our SST-2 profiles illustrate the second case: Masks change while the utility gap stays below one percentage point, so evidence instability and immediate utility loss are distinct findings and should be reported separately.

Function-space ablation is the most direct control and the most expensive, since the ablation requires a forward evaluation per candidate component. The path-normalized score is nearly free and cancels reciprocal scalar gauges exactly. Canonical balancing fixes the coordinate before measuring and therefore lets an existing diagnostic be reused unchanged. None of these three controls addresses non-diagonal G ​ L ​ ( r ) GL(r) mixing; when the audited gauge includes a basis rotation, the control has to be defined on the quotient, as in Corollary 1 .

If the decision is stable across all three profiles, the diagnostic may be reported as evidence about the learned function under the audited symmetry. If the decision changes under the aggressive profile only, the diagnostic is not identifiable on the full orbit but may still be usable when the coordinate is pinned by an explicit convention, which should then be stated wherever the score is reported. If the decision changes under the mild profile, the diagnostic should be canonicalized before use or replaced by a quotient-space score, because coordinate variation of the size already present in ordinary checkpoints is enough to change the conclusion.

The main limitation of this work is the scope of the empirical evaluation. The audits cover encoder classifiers on four GLUE tasks, a ViT on CIFAR-10, three decoder-only language models and a SwiGLU MLP channel audit on WikiText-2, and six trained LoRA adapters, which is a broad but still finite selection rather than a sweep over all datasets, model families, and model scales. Coverage is also uneven across workflows: The vision, decoder-only, and MLP audits use fewer model–task combinations than the GLUE sweep, and the iterative pruning curves are centered on RoBERTa and MRPC. Because the audited symmetries are exact and architecture-native rather than checkpoint-specific, the same reliability concern applies to settings we did not run, and extending the audit to further benchmarks, larger models, and additional gradient-based workflows is direct future work.
